title: What is the EY and EY-Parthenon interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: How EY consulting and its strategy arm EY-Parthenon hire: two to three rounds of behavioural, case and group case interviews, and how to prepare.
hook: EY's interview process depends on the service line and office: EY says the style, format and number of rounds are based on business needs, and may include recorded video, live video and case interviews. EY-Parthenon, its strategy and transactions arm, runs a case-heavy process, usually two or three rounds of candidate-led cases and behavioural interviews, with a strong investor lens. Here is what to expect from each and how to prepare.
body:
Which EY are you applying to?

EY lists its early-career service lines in the US as Assurance, Consulting, EY-Parthenon and Tax. Consulting covers technology, business transformation, risk and people work. EY-Parthenon is the strategy arm: it was built on The Parthenon Group, which EY acquired in 2014, and in March 2025 it absorbed EY's wider Strategy and Transactions business, taking it to more than 25,000 people. Its work now spans corporate strategy, deal strategy and due diligence, and transactions support.

That matters for preparation. A Consulting role may emphasise competency questions and delivery-focused cases; an EY-Parthenon strategy role will test you much as MBB would, often on investment and acquisition questions.

What EY says about its process

EY's US early-careers guidance says the style, format and number of interview rounds depend on business needs, and that interviews may include prerecorded video, live video and case study interviews. It also asks US applicants to apply for no more than two jobs within a six-month period, so choose carefully. Other countries publish their own processes; check the careers page for your office.

The usual EY-Parthenon process

Offices that publish their process typically run two or three rounds. A common shape:

  1. Application, with an online or in-person test in some offices.
  2. First round: case interviews, often with behavioural questions at the start, usually with consultants or managers.
  3. Final round: further cases and a behavioural interview with directors or partners, where motivation for EY-Parthenon carries real weight.

Graduate routes in some countries add an online assessment and an assessment day that may include a group exercise; some offices use a written case. Your invitation will tell you which.

The cases

EY-Parthenon cases are usually candidate-led, similar in style to BCG and Bain: you clarify, structure, ask for data, do the maths and recommend. Because of the transactions work, cases often have an investor lens: should a client buy this business, is this market attractive to a private equity buyer, what is this company worth? Expect data-heavy questions where you must pick out what matters. Useful background: the complete guide to M&A cases and private equity cases.

A worked example: should a food producer buy its distributor?

(Illustrative numbers.) A regional food producer is considering buying the distributor that delivers its products. The distributor earns $3M of EBITDA a year, and comparable businesses sell for about 6x EBITDA.

  • Rough value of the distributor: $3M × 6 = $18M. That is a reference point, not a price: debt, working capital and integration risk all matter.
  • Buying it would save the producer about $1M a year in distribution margin. At the same 6x multiple, that saving is worth about $1M × 6 = $6M in value.
  • But the deal needs $4M of extra working capital, and other producers who use the distributor may leave rather than ship through a competitor. If they supply $1.5M of its EBITDA and half of them leave, EBITDA falls by $1.5M × 50% = $0.75M, worth $0.75M × 6 = $4.5M.
  • So the synergy value of $6M shrinks to about $6M − $4.5M = $1.5M, before the $4M of working capital is even counted.

Vertical integration looks less obvious now. The right comparison is against alternatives, such as renegotiating terms or switching distributor.

Weak: "The distributor is worth $18M and saves us $1M a year, so we should buy it."
Strong: "The $1M of savings is worth about $6M, but losing half the other producers could wipe out $4.5M of that, and we would tie up $4M in working capital. Unless we can keep those producers, renegotiating our contract looks better value. I'd test how they would react before going further."

How to prepare

  • Prepare as you would for MBB: structure, driving the case, clean maths and a clear recommendation. How to drive a case.
  • Get comfortable with deal concepts: EBITDA multiples, synergies, working capital and due diligence questions.
  • Give behavioural preparation equal time to cases, with several real stories and a specific answer to why EY-Parthenon.
  • Practise a group case and a written case if your office uses them. How group and written cases work.

Common mistakes

  • Treating a valuation multiple as a recommendation. "$18M" answers what it might cost, not whether to buy it.
  • Forgetting dis-synergies. Customers, suppliers or partners can walk away after a deal.
  • Generic motivation. Say why the mix of strategy and transactions work at EY-Parthenon appeals to you specifically.
  • Relying on one published process. Numbers of rounds and tests vary by office; confirm with your recruiter.

Practice

The producer manages to keep all the other producers. What is the synergy value now, and how long would the $1M annual saving take to repay the $4M of working capital?

Show the answer

With no lost EBITDA, the synergy value is the full $1M × 6 = $6M. The working capital takes $4M ÷ $1M = 4 years to repay from the savings alone. The deal still needs a purchase price that leaves room for that.

Where to go next

Compare with PwC and Strategy& and continue with the KPMG process.
